                                                         Abstract
               We give a randomized algorithmic version of the Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem for sets
          of integers. Let A ⊆ [N ] have size n := |A| ≥ 2, let 1 ≤ K ≤ n, and suppose that its additive
          energy satisfies E(A) ≥ n3 /K. Reiher and Schoen proved existentially√          that, for every fixed

                           √  is a subset A   ⊆ A satisfying |A   | ≥ (1 − ϵ)n/  K and |A  − A′ | ≤ Oϵ (K 4 )|A′ |;
          the size scale n/ K is essentially optimal. We give an algorithmic counterpart: with probability
          at least 1 −√n−10 , our algorithm runs in time nKN o(1) and returns a subset A′ ⊆ A satisfying
          |A′ | ≥ cn/ K and |A′ − A′ | ≤ CK 4 |A′ |, where c, C > 0 are absolute constants. Thus the
          output attains the essentially optimal subset-size scale and the best-known K 4 dependence for
          the normalized difference set.


1        Introduction
The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle [BS94, Gow98] converts high additive energy into a large
subset with controlled additive growth. For a set A ⊆ [N ] of size n, its additive energy E(A) is
the number of ordered quadruples (a1 , a2 , a3 , a4 ) ∈ A4 satisfying a1 + a2 = a3 + a4 ; thus 2n2 − n ≤
E(A) ≤ n3 . Balog and Szemerédi [BS94] first proved that the hypothesis E(A) ≥ n3 /K forces a
large subset with small additive growth. Gowers [Gow98, Proposition 12] replaced the regularity-
based quantitative dependence by polynomial bounds. Tracking the constants in his proof under
E(A) ≥ n3 /K gives a subset A′ ⊆ A with |A′ | ≥ n/(219 K 12 ) and |A′ − A′ | ≤ 238 nK 24 ; equivalently,
|A′ − A′ | = O(K 36 |A′ |). Reiher and Schoen [RS24, Theorem√1.2] later proved that, for every fixed
ϵ ∈√(0, 1/2), one can simultaneously achieve |A′ | ≥ (1 − ϵ)n/ K and |A′ − A′ | ≤ Oϵ (K 4 )|A′ |. Their
n/ K size scale is essentially optimal in order of magnitude. The coordinate-axis example of Reiher
and Schoen [RS24] is stated over finite abelian groups and gives the sharp leading constant there.
For an integer analogue, fix r and M ≫ r, and let A0 ⊆ Zr be the union of the coordinate intervals
{tei : 1 ≤ t ≤ M }, where ei is the ith standard basis vector. Then |A0 | = rM and E(A0 ) = Θ(rM 3 ),
so K = Θ(r2 ), while, for every fixed δ > 0, every subset of more than (1+δ)M elements has Ωδ (M 2 )
distinct cross-axis differences. A sufficiently large-base encoding of the containing box into Z is
a Freiman 2-isomorphism, so it preserves equality among differences and       √ hence preserves both
additive energy and difference-set cardinalities. Thus, for integer sets, n/ K is the correct order of
magnitude for the largest subset A′ satisfying |A′ − A′ | = OK (|A′ |); this transfer does not preserve
the sharp leading constant 1. The exponent 4 is best known but is not proved optimal: the examples
discussed in [RS24] only rule out replacing it by an exponent smaller than log(4)/ log(27/16) ≈
2.649.

in O(nK 28 poly log N ) time which returns a set A′ ⊆ A with |A′ | ≥ Ω(n/K 2 ) and |A′ + A′ | ≤
O(nK 28 ) = O(K 30 |A′ |). Independently, Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [ABF23, Theorem 3.3]
give a randomized algorithm running in O(nK e      12 ) time and returning a set of size Ω(n/K 2 ) with |A′ +

A′ | ≤ O(nK 24 ) = O(K 26 |A′ |). Fischer, Jin, and Xu [FJX25, Theorem 1.11] obtain a deterministic
algorithm running in (n2 /K 2 + K 13 n)N o(1) time and returning a set of size at least n/(64K) with
|A′ + A′ | ≤ K 16 nN o(1) = O(K 17 N o(1) )|A′ |. Thus, prior √algorithms either have a large polynomial
dependence on K, return a set below the existential n/ K scale, or incur a substantially weaker
normalized additive bound.
     It is natural to ask the following question.

         Is it possible to design an nKN  o(1) -time algorithm that returns a set A′ ⊆ A with
                                         √
                             |A′ | ≥ Ω(n/ K) and |A′ − A′ | ≤ O(K 4 )|A′ |?

In this paper, we give a positive answer to this question.

1.1    Our results
We now state our main result in compact form, followed by a brief explanation of its proof and its
comparison with the closest previous bounds. The complete statements and proofs appear later in
the paper.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal version of Theorem 5.1). Let A ⊆ [N ] be a set of n ≥ 2 integers, let
1 ≤ K ≤ n, and suppose that E(A) ≥ n3 /K. There is a randomized algorithm which, with
probability at least 1 − n−10 , runs in time nKN o(1) and returns a set A′ ⊆ A such that
                                      √
                         |A′ | ≥ Ω(n/ K)      and      |A′ − A′ | ≤ O(K 4 )|A′ |.

We first use the deterministic popular-sums approximation of Lemma 3.3 with additive error
Θ(n/K). Discarding differences below a constant multiple of this error loses only a small    √ con-

the high-multiplicity part carries a constant fraction of the

differences finds an energetic translate Ad of size Ω(n/ K), and the cleaning argument gives the
stronger normalized difference bound O(K 3 ). Otherwise the low-multiplicity part carries a constant

                                                                           √        5.1 combines its
multiplicity levels into a thresholded tail whose relation has density Ω(1/ K) and √  whose support

Thus Theorem 1.1 reaches, up to absolute constants, the essentially optimal existential size scale
and the best-known K 4 dependence for the normalized difference set. Corollary 5.2 gives the
corresponding bound |A′ + A′ | ≤ CK 8 |A′ |. Since the theorem is randomized and one-set, it does
not replace the asymmetric deterministic BSG theorem required in some applications.
